"Pneumatic" describes anything that involves air or gas — almost always compressed air (ordinary air that has been squeezed under high pressure). When something is called pneumatic, it either uses compressed air to work, is filled with compressed air, or simply relates to air or gas in some meaningful way.

A helpful analogy: just as "electric" tells you something works using electricity, "pneumatic" tells you something works using compressed air.
1. Powered or operated by compressed air

This is the most common use of the word. Pneumatic tools and machines are driven by pressurized air rather than a traditional motor or electricity alone.

These tools are usually connected to an air compressor — a machine that takes in ordinary air and squeezes it into a tank at very high pressure. That stored pressure is then released in bursts to do powerful, rapid work.

Examples:

  • A pneumatic drill (also called a jackhammer) — the loud, heavy machine construction workers use to break up concrete. It works by driving a pointed metal bit up and down at tremendous force, powered entirely by bursts of compressed air.
  • A pneumatic nail gun — fires nails into wood using a sharp burst of air pressure.
  • A pneumatic wrench — tightens or loosens bolts at high speed using compressed air, commonly used in car repair shops.
  • A pneumatic press — uses air pressure to stamp, cut, or shape materials in manufacturing.

The defining trait of all these tools is that compressed air is the engine powering the action.

Something can also be called pneumatic simply because it is inflated with air under pressure, where that trapped air gives the object its shape, strength, or function.

Examples:

  • Pneumatic tires — the tires on your bicycle, motorcycle, or car. Inside the rubber, air is compressed to a specific pressure. This pressurized air is what makes the tire firm, supports the vehicle's weight, and cushions you from bumps in the road.
  • Pneumatic cushions and air mattresses — inflated structures that use trapped air for comfort or support.

A pneumatic system can also push or pull objects through tubes using the force of moving air — either blowing them forward (positive pressure) or sucking them along (negative pressure, like a vacuum).

You may have seen this in action at bank drive-throughs, where a small cylinder carrying your documents is shot through a tube to the teller inside and sent back in seconds. This is a pneumatic tube system. Hospitals, large office buildings, and warehouses have long used these to quickly move documents, medicine, small packages, and lab samples across large distances without anyone having to carry them.
4. Relating to air and gas in science and engineering (technical use)

More broadly, "pneumatic" is used as a technical descriptor in physics, engineering, and biology to describe anything that involves the behavior or properties of air and gases.

  • Pneumatic pressure = air pressure
  • Pneumatic system = any system that uses compressed air to transmit force or do work. Large trucks and buses, for example, use pneumatic braking systems, where compressed air presses the brake pads rather than hydraulic fluid.
  • Pneumatic conveying = a method used in factories to move bulk materials (like grain, powder, or chemicals) through pipes using a strong flow of air.
  • Pneumatic bones = in anatomy, bones that have hollow, air-filled spaces inside them rather than being solid. Several bones in the human skull — and in birds — are pneumatic. In birds especially, many bones are air-filled, which dramatically reduces their weight and makes flying possible.

5. Relating to the spirit or soul (rare, specialized, philosophical/theological)

In theology and philosophy — especially in early Christian thought and Gnostic writings — "pneumatic" was used to describe things relating to the spirit or the divine breath. A "pneumatic" person, in this old philosophical sense, was someone believed to be guided by spiritual forces rather than just the body or rational mind. You are most likely to encounter this use when reading old religious texts or philosophical works. It is rarely used this way in modern everyday English.
6. Describing a full, rounded body shape (informal, dated)

In informal and literary English — especially in British usage from the early-to-mid 20th century — "pneumatic" was sometimes used to describe a person's body as full, rounded, and pleasingly curved, the way an inflated tire is round and firm. The writer Aldous Huxley used it this way in his novel Brave New World. This usage is quite rare in modern English, but worth knowing if you encounter it in older literature.
The single thread connecting every use

No matter where you see "pneumatic," the connecting idea is always air:

  • Air doing work (drills, nail guns, wrenches)
  • Air providing structure (tires, mattresses)
  • Air moving things (tube systems, conveying)
  • Air spaces inside something (pneumatic bones)
  • The metaphorical "breath" of the spirit (theological use)
  • The fullness of something air-inflated (informal body description)
How to interpret it when you see it

Whenever "pneumatic" appears in front of a noun, ask yourself: "Is this thing powered by compressed air, filled with air, or does it involve air in some meaningful way?" That single question will almost always unlock the correct interpretation.

  • "Pneumatic conveyor" → moves materials using air
  • "Pneumatic tires" → tires filled with pressurized air
  • "Pneumatic braking system" → brakes operated by compressed air
  • "Pneumatic drill" → drill powered by compressed air
  • "Pneumatic bones" → bones with air-filled hollow spaces inside

The word essentially stamps a piece of technology, a body part, or a system and announces: air is what makes this work, or air is what defines this.
